And cut off vague answers as soon as we can, assumptions, presumptions, conclusions, and let's get to the facts as quickly as we can. We'll take a break first, and we will resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before the witness enters the courtroom, could the Defence pay attention specifically to the translation of D768. Initially there was no translation. Then later it was introduced through another witness. We asked several times for an update on the availability of the English translation, and I think we have not received any answer. So if the Defence would revisit this matter and tell us -- update --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then preferably this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First we would like to offer the previous document but the OTP version into evidence. It's 65 ter 32617.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Surprise, surprise. Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have 1D05443 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the translation of this document, Mr. Misic, so could you please read what this is.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: This is -- these are the rules on the central records of missing persons for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any chance that would you have an English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We'll double-check, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So tell us who enacted this document and on what basis? Because we don't have the translation, just read the preamble before the title.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: This is a bylaw. "Pursuant to Article 23, paras 2 and 5 of the Law on Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, issue number 50/04, and Article 18 and Article 36 of the statute of the missing persons institute of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 01-40-UO-122/07, dated 2nd August 2007, the board of management of the Institute of Missing Persons for Bosnia-Herzegovina with the consent of the founders adopted at its 28th Session held on 5 December 2008 the following rules ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does your institute work according to these rules?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: These rules elaborated how the process of verification should proceed, and it contains the provisions that I mentioned earlier; namely, that verifications had been done based on documents that these rules do not recognise. Also, the rules envisaged that three registers should be made. The first would be a register of verified persons, including the legally prescribed minimum of information; second, the register of unverified persons; and third, the register of deleted persons. Unfortunately, we did not make any of the three registers in keeping with these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 9. We need paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it because we have no translation. Article 21: "Conclusion on Verification. "(1) When the commission, after cross-checking and verifying the information for the purposes of Articles 12 to 21 of the rules, has established that the information on the missing persons matches, the commission will adopt the conclusion on verification and establish a unified verification number (INO number). "(2) the collegium shall determine the contents and the format of the conclusion referred to in para (1) of this article and that shall be an integral part of the rules." Would you please explain the significance of this article.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Well, this article stipulates on the basis of which documents information about a missing person can be verified and which data is to be verified. Until 2013, I believe - and I'm now talking about para (2) of this article - the previous collegium of directors had prescribed what minutes should contain and what the conclusions should be and that was below the minimum of information prescribed by the law. And I believe it was in 2013 that we changed the guide-lines and we adopted a new format on the basis of which to verify the legally prescribed minimum of information. It was not perfect but at least we had come to some sort of agreement. It was not completely in conformity with these rules, but it was acceptable to all the three members of the collegium, and we had managed to find a comprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Lukic - but I'm also looking at you, Mr. Jeremy - the flawed results of this institute, as the witness presented to us, where does the Prosecution rely on it? And I'm asking you as well, Mr. Lukic, because if it affects other evidence, then, of course, it's very relevant. If it's -- if there's no evidence which relies on this flawed information, then it would not affect the evidence and then it's -- becomes rather irrelevant to hear what an institute produced for bad results, results not known to us and not in evidence. Could you please tell us where and what experts? And for example, I just looked at something we heard recently; that is, for example, the Tomasica report of Ms. Tabeau, I don't think she uses this as one of the sources. But I may miss something because there were a lot of cross-references here and there. Could I ask you, Mr. Lukic, first of all, what evidence you are challenging through these flaws in the work of this institute?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I continue through the questions to this witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I want to have an answer to that, and then, of course, you can continue if it turns out to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would still insist to ask this witness. I think he is more knowledgeable than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are the one who calls the witness and you are the one who is in a position to determine the relevance of the evidence you are presenting. The witness can't do that. And the witness wouldn't know where in the evidence of this case one of the parties relied on the results of their work. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I rise because you also addressed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, it's -- it's for the relevance, of course, I'm asking you as well whether somewhere you rely on the now-challenged results of the work of this institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My -- the understanding of the Prosecution is that the -- in terms of material that has been generated by the missing persons institute, which is relied on by the Prosecution or Prosecution experts in this case, what we're talking about is the report on the municipalities, the death report prepared by Witness Ewa Tabeau, that's P2797. And within that report, she relies as the sources that she looked at on 193 missing persons certificates that were provided by the missing persons institute, and I would add that she relies on those never as a single source, and I also understand there are an additional 30 missing persons certificates from the missing persons institute that were bar tabled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we are talking about a number of cases Ms. Tabeau relied upon in the municipalities report where she doesn't use this institute's report as exclusive sources but as cross-references -- cross-referenced them with other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Of the five and a half thousand documents or so that she relies on in that report, the missing persons institute certificates make up 193 of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we know at least what we're talking about. Mr. Lukic, that's apparently where the evidence of this witness gains some relevance. Would you then please focus on, for example, what the flaws are and to what extent this is not repaired by the cross-referencing of Ms. Tabeau. For example -- I'm not saying that that's the case, but if for example you'd say the name of the mother was missing, that even all the other sources Tabeau uses, the mother's name is mentioned, then it -- the impact may be less. The mere fact, Mr. Lukic, that you couldn't immediately give an answer whereas Mr. Jeremy gave an answer, I don't know whether it's the complete answer or not, is of some concern to this Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Misic, which institutions use your information? What about your co-operation with the ICMP and the courts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Our information is used -- well, the law envisaged that all institutions could use our information, but it's mainly the ones who are verified; that is to say, the judicial institutions, the authorities, the courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina which deal with cases involving that information, or courts dealing with cases that have to establish certain entitlements or cases before the prosecutor's office for war crimes of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll cite some specific examples later. But to answer in more general terms Judge Orie's question now, when establishing the date and place of disappearance or death a mistake is made, could that replicate the mistake in other institutions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Because we are the only institution authorised to established this information about the circumstances, the time and place of disappearance, when we make an error, it's very important. We do our job using all the records available, including all the records that were kept on missing persons, and I've named them already: The ICRC one commission; the second commission; and the ICMP. And I say with full responsibility that every database, every database, has a lot of flaws, a lot of shortcomings, and the purpose of the verification commission is to cross-check all these databases mutually and get to correct information. Let me just tell you this. ICMP established one database that was included in the central records of missing persons, but we have one problem with that: That database, apart from containing a lot of inaccuracies on key elements, also contains a number of elements that are not subject to verification at all, so that database can sometimes create a false picture of a missing person on key parameters that I mentioned. I also want to add that these databases containing inaccurate information without one consent, and that is another deficiency in the implementation of this law, are being used by courts which, at the request of families, proclaim a missing person dead, and while doing so, they do not take the trouble to ascertain all these things that I've mentioned. So it happens occasionally that concerning one individual in three different databases, we have a place and time and circumstances of disappearance which the court was not aware of at all when it was making its decision. And the court makes its decision and proclaims the person as dead as of a certain date - let's say the 11th of July - and in three databases, we have information that that person had disappeared, had gone missing in 1993 or 1994. The problem is that if we don't do that job till the end, then somebody else deals with it - like the courts are doing now - in a chaotic way, and what should be the purpose, the end purpose of the central records on missing persons is just not achieved, and that purpose is to find out the truth about every individual. So now we are in a situation where we have to note that various sorts of manipulation are going on with these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a question. Sir, you told us before the break of just how difficult it is in your institution to come up with proper records of the missing persons because there are people who are obstructing this information, and you told us that people are said to have died during the war when they haven't. Now, this time now you're telling us about same problems about -- from -- with the ICMP. What I want to find out from you, and you say the ICMP also gives incorrect information, how do you determine that the ICMP information is incorrect when you yourself don't have the correct information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our duty to establish information as accurately as possible. That is why I said that there is no completely accurate database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand your duty. Let me stop you. I understand your duty. I want you to explain to me how you implement that duty. Your duty is to make sure that the information is correct. Now you don't have correct information. You're criticising another institution for giving incorrect information, how do you determine that that information from that other institution is incorrect if you yourself don't have correct information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it is our duty to compare all databases and all registers. We are the ones who are at the position to do so rather than other institutions providing databases. We are in charge of keeping information about persons from registers that were and still are being kept in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, there's a person on the ICMP database who is considered missing, and we run checks through certain records kept in Bosnia-Herzegovina to establish that the person in question is alive. So it is a procedure prescribed by the law. We are the ones who are supposed to do that in a complete way so as to be able to say these lists and those registers are accurate. So we check whatever we receive, and the ICMP provides input to that database without having carried out previous checks, as did other institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. You're telling me the law and what you are supposed to do, and I said I do understand that's what you're supposed to do. That's your duty. What I'm asking you is -- I'm saying to you, you told us this morning how chaotic things are in your institution. People are doing things for their own benefit and not doing it according to the law. Now, the result is, and you told us this this morning, that as a result the information you have about missing people is incorrect and incomplete. Now, my question to you is if you working on the basis of incorrect and incomplete information, how do you come to the conclusion that the work of another institution whose processes you don't know is incorrect? You can only say something is wrong if you can tell me what the right thing is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I can say that they are wrong. I can prove they are. If we are to discuss any base, database --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then if you can prove they are, then you must have the truth. But you don't by your own admission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I said was that we started the verification process in a poor way. I mentioned the 10.000-plus people for whom the procedure was not undertaken entailing all the checks I mentioned. As of 2013 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've also told us that you haven't verified because you are unable to complete this job because of the problems that you're having.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I mentioned the 10.000-plus people. After that, we amended our regulation. And in terms of some 7.000 people, we established what I mentioned here. I said that there are shortcomings there as well but that the process was significantly improved precisely because for every person processed under the new rules and regulations, since I am a member of the collegium, checks were done in the databases of other bodies and authorities in terms of registers kept in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I told you there is no completely accurate database. That is why all information must be checked. Once verification is complete, once we have conducted all the checks for the person in question, then that person may be considered fully verified. Just so that you do not misunderstand me. What I'm saying is that, yes, we do have omissions in the process of verification which occurred before 2013. After that, when we employed a different modus operandi, we established that no database was accurate, which is something to be expected. However, our problem is that we no longer go back to check the 10.000-plus people so that we apply the correct legal procedure so that we are able say that list is accurate because the analysis was conducted by the competent institution. Because of those wrong findings, municipal courts work the way I explained. I reiterate that the courts do not take into account all the relevant documents and information about missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You've gone far beyond my question. Just this morning I said to you -- based on the information you told us about the situation in your institution, I said to you: Isn't it better that we just pack and go home, and you said that would be a good solution. Now you are saying to us that you had initial problems, you have improved on them, 7.000 are now better out of 10.000, and things are going according to law. This doesn't accord with what you told us this morning because this morning the problem was perpetuating even as we speak; that is, this gentleman who you mentioned who is frustrating everything. So I'm just saying to you, I'm finding it a little difficult to follow your evidence now because I'm not sure I -- we are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? I stand by what I said previously. It's better that we do nothing and disband if we are unwilling to verify the 10.000-plus as prescribed by the law. That is the problem in terms of this obstruction. Well, we may leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed, and let's try to get to the core of the relevance of the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was. I thought to go through the legislation first, but obviously I'll have to jump to the concrete cases so maybe it would be easier, understandable for everybody. So I would offer this document and actually to ask this document to be MFI'd since there is no translation. And it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1095, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D5388, please. I think that we should have translation for this document. Yeah, this is -- the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can that be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May be better to stay without broadcasting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public, therefore. And then perhaps everyone reads what this record is about. As far as the name of the person concerned, we have it on our screens now, and that we refer to "this person." Please proceed. And, Mr. Jeremy, could you check whether this is one of the 193 Ms. Tabeau relied upon. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would start with page 36 from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment we have English on both sides of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's just cover page for the names, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Same person on either side?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no. We have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without mentioning the name of the person, Mr. Misic, since we don't want the names to be known publicly -- well, you can see who the person in question is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have English on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's that kind of form. There are bilingual. We have B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Misic, kindly start your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: We need to look at other documents in terms of this person as well to understand my point. We see here the circumstances and time of disappearance as well as the date when the report is submitted. So we need to take note of that in order to understand the issue on hand. Am I going to read out the circumstances, because it may identify the person?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a general information.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: After -- on the 13th of March, 1993, the sought person disappeared after the RS person took over (redacted) She stayed -- I'm sorry, I touched the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the report was submitted in February 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If would you not to read out aloud the possible identifying elements such as the exact village, we don't need it, I take it, for your explanation. So that she stayed in her house, and we'll not read where that was, where other inhabitants ran away. That's the circumstances contained in this ICRC report. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an ICMP document.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document is the same as the previous one in terms of date and place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the next page, please. We have this page in English only but we will need it in both versions. Page 39 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this page, we have an ICMP comment when they took blood samples from members of the family. They also created a file that information can be extracted from. So previously we had information about the person from two previous databases, those of the ICMP and the ICRC. Here we have additional information as well as explanation provided by the ICMP. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. On the first document, it says that she disappeared on the 13th of March, 1993, after the attack by the VRS in (redacted) We see here that she was killed and buried in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let us move on because there are further databases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third primary database. More or less, the data is the same. Let us move on to reach the final document. So we have three databases so far with approximately similar information. So this person should have been verified according to the information we have seen thus far, but let us go to the next document. So we have the three primary databases which were entered in the central records of missing persons. This person was verified pursuant to the record of identification, which was not done pursuant to the law. There we find that she went missing on the 17th of July, 1995. So this is completely off. She is one of the 10.000-plus people. So verification was done circumventing the legally prescribed method. This document is not recognised by the law, and information contained therein is completely inaccurate, creating a completely wrong picture of how this person disappeared. This document was also signed by a representative of the competent prosecutor's office. So when they create this record of identification, they do not carry out background checks. If the procedure had been followed under the law, there would have been no problem legally speaking, but further work was carried out based on a document which was completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now before the break, let us look at a few more pages in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Just to come back to you on your query. So the individual that we were looking at isn't encompassed within the 193 missing persons certificates that I referred to as -- that were referenced in Ms. Tabeau's report, although that relates to the municipalities rather than Srebrenica. Here we're looking at documents that I understand do not originate from the missing persons institute about relate to Srebrenica missing, and the individual that we're looking at here isn't included in the report relating to Srebrenica missing, P1901.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever mistakes there may have been made, it has no effect as far as you are concerned on the evidence which is before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. I mean, if mistakes are made, of course our great concern is whether it affects the reliability of the evidence before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, because it is always implied in the majority of the cases that these killed persons are killed in connection with Srebrenica killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if nowhere this faulty document was relied upon, then at least that mistake has been avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe not by Ms. Tabeau. But we have ICMP lists of killed persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then what we need to establish to find that there is an effect, we should see a record by this institute which is then copied, duplicated in the ICMP records, and then see whether the mistakes are copied. Now, I do understand that here the ICMP data are different from what is found in this report signed by this institute. So therefore, in this case, apparently, it has not had any effect on the ICMP records. That's how I understand it, but ... I mean, just establishing somewhere in the world mistakes were made which are to some extent related to what happened in the Balkans 1992, 1995, is not sufficient to make it relevant for our case. What we need is that it effects the reliability of the evidence which is before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are establishing relevance, and we will have demographer who would go into details. I cannot go into details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if it's not related in any way to the evidence before us, it could not affect the reliability of that evidence irrespective of what a demographer will tell us unless that demographer is going to tell us that this information slipped in somewhere. And that's the reason why I asked you that question, where does it affect the reliability of the evidence as it is before us; that is, the evidence presented by the Prosecution. Please proceed, but keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to jump from one question to another because I'm really pushed hard today. I had my very smooth flow, but I'll try to accommodate you. We'll need to see 1D05786, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we leave this document, can we confirm that this document comes -- the institute it comes from is the Tuzla clinic centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can ask the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, what institution produced that document that we just looked at, as we saw that it was at the Tuzla clinic centre or clinical centre, as was translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Don't look at the screen. It was related to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's the previous document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document from the clinical centre of Tuzla. It's their regular format, and it's about the final identification of a person based on a DNA report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You have answered my question. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can that be broadcast? What we have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. You should always first indicate if it can be broadcast or not. Then it should not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Mr. Misic, before us we have a document, and we won't mention the name. What can you tell us about this document of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Again, it's a document from only one database, and that's not enough for a person to be verified. However, all the documents we are looking at, when one and the same person is in issue, the information about the dates and place and circumstances of disappearance differ from one database to another. We see that this person has not been verified, but the problem is that this document is completely inaccurate, although it was generated in May 1996. It's inaccurate according to our checks. I don't know if I need to explain. This person died as the result of an accident, not in the way it's stated here, and it should have been rejected as a missing person. The report of a missing person was incorrect. And I'm telling you there are many cases like this, in the federal commission, in the Republika Srpska database, in the ICRC base. We can talk about missing persons only about the basis of the central register. This person died after the war in a misadventure. He was killed accidentally by a member of his own unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you specify when was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] December 1995, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And when did your institution receive the information about his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was killed by accident. I can't tell you exactly when we received the report, but we ran checks on this person looking at all the documents that were available about him, and then we established that this report was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When was this check carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last year, I believe. And that person was not verified. He should be entered into the list of unverified persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was the information about his death available to the institute on the 23rd of May, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How can you say that this is a wrong certificate, what we have on the screen now? Because, at that time - May 1996 - the information about his death was not available. It states here only that he was, at that time, missing. Or did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every report, including this one, is subject to our verification. We carried out checks on this person, and the information we found out is that he didn't disappear on this date, he didn't disappear in this place, and the circumstances are completely wrong. In December 1995, he was patrolling along the separation line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the person who submitted this report that was after the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But at the beginning, you gave the impression that this was a kind of false information contained in this document. At that time, it was not false because it was not known. You agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might have been a mistake, but what I'm trying to say again is that not a single list, not a single database, not a single name could pass without complete verification. Not even the ICMP. I don't know how this report came about, whether it was deliberate manipulation. It could be. I don't know for a fact. But in any case, not a single list can be considered as correct until we have carried out our verifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment we are not discussing a list but this document. How can you say it could be a deliberate manipulation if you yourself say at that time, when this document was created, it was not known that this person died by an accident or a killing? How could it be a deliberate manipulation if the facts were not known to those who reported him missing? And I'm talking about May 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if I remember well about this person, I described to you the circumstances. I know them. If he really died under the circumstances that I know, he couldn't have been found in a mass grave. There's no way that a person who is accidentally killed by a member of his own unit ended up in a mass grave. I'm trying to tell you nothing is correct until a full verification is carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stop you. Please tell me where I can find any mentioning of a mass grave in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 6 of this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's go on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes please. But the witness is talking about this document as it is on the screen now. And then please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, because you didn't have a chance to see the whole document. It's -- no, I mean, the bad side of this electronic version, but at page 6 we'll see the list, and it's mentioned graveyard 634 where 112 persons were exhumed. And under yellow underline, has underlined this person from the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a slightly unconnected question. What is the name of the unit of this person which a member of whom killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was one of the medical units of the 28th Division from Srebrenica. He was a member of a medical company or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And on what date was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's somewhere in the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date. December 1995. I know it was after the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where was the 28th Division at that time, on that day? Or the medical unit of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to the information that became available to us, they were on the separation line on patrol duty, at least some of the members of the 28th Division were on patrol duty. By that time, the 28th Division had been reorganised to some extent. They were involved in reconnaissance activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On what date in December 1995 was the 28th Division at that place on the reconnaissance mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is in the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th of December, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next document tells us about the whereabouts of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's about the activities of a part of the 28th Division which wasn't called the 28th Division at that time. Not all of their units were engaged. The operative units were not involved in types of -- in -- in this type of task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think it would be better that we allow you now to continue. What we could do is to continue for another ten minutes, then adjourn for the day because -- not to take any further break. And that you take us page by page through this document. And, of course, having a slightly longer session but an earlier break would, of course, be -- Mr. Mladic should agree with that. If not, then we'll take a break and then we'll have the ten minutes later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud. Mr. Lukic, does Mr. Mladic agree that we continue for another ten minutes and then adjourn for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you take us page by page through this document. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just a question for Mr. Lukic necessitated by the lack of a translation. There's been a reference to accidental killing, and I just wonder if that is included in the B/C/S documents and perhaps there isn't an English translation of it. I don't see it in the documents that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see at least something from a university clinic on the second page. Is that the one? But, please take us through the document and -- so that we know where potential problems are. It's indeed that problem that we don't have an English translation, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is. I know. I'm aware of it. But this document came late. I just today asked you to add it on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we -- we saw the first page. Can we see the second page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this document, we also see that he was killed on the 12th of July, 1995. It was issued on the 27th of November, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. This is precisely what I was referring to. Somebody manipulates information with a certain intent, or perhaps unintentionally, in terms of circumstances and time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to advise you, my learned friend Mr. Jeremy also raised the issue. In the documents that I have and which was uploaded in the system, I did not come across manslaughter; that is to say, the unintentional killing by a member of his unit in December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: Then I have to direct you to the monograph of the 28th Division produced by a group of authors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, reference was made to a date in November. Where do we find a date in November on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: November? I said April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, let me just see. It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- "On this document we also see that he was killed on the 12th of July. It was issued on the 27th of November ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: April. Okay, yes. Then I understand it, Mr. Lukic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what does it then say? So this document again repeats that he was killed on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's one day after than the first one. But it's not a big issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And where do we find that exactly so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first one is 11th -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- I'm just trying to find that date. I see it's in green, 12th/7/1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous page is 11th July 1995, previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And this comes from a university clinic in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could the witness read what the place is where this person is supposed to have died? It says "mijesto."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Snagovo, Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you confirm that this document comes from a clinical centre and states that this person, (redacted) (redacted) died on the 12th of July, 1995, in Zvornik. Is that what the document tells us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was signed by members of the family, a representative of the prosecutor's office, and a representative of the institute. The date is stated as we can see here. Through additional checks, it was established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, why not answer my question? Does the document state that this person died on the 12th of July in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what we can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then there are three names at the bottom. The first, is that a reference to a family member?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we scroll down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where it starts on the left, there are three columns at the bottom. The very left starting with "identitet." What does that mean? Is that a family member or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the lower part, there's a friend's name and it states that one of the parents confirmed the identity. Towards the top, it was signed by a forensic pathologist and the authorised official who is usually a representative of the cantonal prosecutor's office in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have the basic in fact about this document now. Mr. Lukic, could you take us to the next page. Oh, but Judge Moloto has one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, can you just confirm is the university clinic in Tuzla the same as the Tuzla clinical centre? Is it one and the same institution or are they two separate institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the same institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do we know enough about this one and go to the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next page is only DNA report. Can we go to next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there's nothing in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if this is a DNA report, from where was the sample taken? Anything to that effect that we know what exactly is compared with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the middle part, Your Honour. We have it in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we see the name of the father between brackets. And we see further down the three persons apparently who gave samples with which they were compared. Now, is there -- yes. And I take it that the site is where the body part or the body was found, that is, in Snagovo, which then was used for a DNA sampling. Is that how we should understand this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least I do understand that way. Maybe the witness could confirm. He has more knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if the witness has any -- is there anything we said until now which is inaccurate, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It makes no sense that the mortal remains were found in the mass grave at Snagovo. They could have only have been found at the place where he died. This person in other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's jumping to conclusions. We are just looking at what this report tells us and whether we made any mistake in summarising what is in this report irrespective of whether it makes sense or not. We'll move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the next page is the same, only has a stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I see the date below the signature, it's different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The signature is different, the date is different, and the -- I think the probability, 99. -- which appears somewhere, I take it that's the probability that it is a match, and that is in many respects, this report, therefore, is different, both in numbers. So apparently it is a different DNA test.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed. If you say it's just the same, Mr. Lukic, it apparently is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no translation of this, Mr. Misic. Therefore, tell us briefly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: This is a file I referred to previously, extracted from the databases kept for the citizens of BiH which had been updated previously in terms of post-war data. So this is a record confirming that a person was alive and then passed away. In other words, it is a result of some checks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who made this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's nothing questionable about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Judge asked you who produced it.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC
utterances.text: It is, as we can see, the report of our state agency about some particulars kept for all inhabitants on citizens of BiH. As the institute, we have access to that data. This one was printed on the 17th of October, 2013. Members of the commission of the institute for missing persons can enter the database and print out this form to confirm that the person existed, passed away, or may still be alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What does this document say? Is the person still alive or did he pass away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we only have the particulars. We don't have that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this apparently refers to a person which once existed and it's extracted from a database. Ready to go to page 6 or should we stop, perhaps, for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question about this document. You said, sir, this -- as we can see the report is of our state agency. How do we -- where do we see in the report that it is of a state agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The acronym IDDEEA. It is the acronym of the state agency which keeps all registers providing the central database for all citizens of BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commission must take a report of this kind into account so as to confirm that the person in question is, indeed, a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the acronym is IDDEEA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. You can see it in the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we see two dates in this document. The one, 20th of April, 1965, is corresponding with the date of birth of this person as we saw it in the other documents. We also see a date, the 3rd of June, 1981. Could you tell us what that date stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3rd of June 1981, I suppose it had to do with the unique personal number of that citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It very much looks like a date and not as a personal number, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date when the number was assigned. You can see the unique number at the very top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it would be best -- unless, Mr. Lukic, you consider it better, and if Mr. Mladic would agree, to go to pages 6 and 7. There are two left. I think 6 we looked at already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I don't know whether you want to go to 7 or adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 7 is just a continuation of 6, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I'll ask one thing from the witness and then, Mr. Lukic, perhaps it would be better to adjourn. And, Witness, could you please read the entry which the chapter which comes immediately after the green highlighted portion, which apparently started "podaci o." You see that is preceding the first entry where the date of the 3rd of June, 1981 appears. Could you read that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is additional information. The municipality Bratunac. The date, the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, date of what? Could you read? It says "datum," and then a word follows. Could you read that out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Date of determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I see a little bit higher up, also preceding the date the 3rd of June, and forgive me for my pronunciation but it -- I would pronounce it as "datum prebivalista." Do you see that? In the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read that so that we receive translation of what it stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Residence date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's when -- yes. We'll adjourn for the day. Mr. Lukic, you'll understand that on the basis of this document, the inconsistency with what seems to be a traffic accident or something like that is not yet there, so I take it that we'll further hear from that tomorrow. We adjourn for the day and with apologies for having gone beyond the time-limit we indicated earlier. Witness, before we adjourn, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony you are still about to give tomorrow. If that is clear to you, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.30, and you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 9th of July, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of July, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.01 p.m.,
